venues.a: Innere Stadt (1st), behind the State Opera
venues.d: The definitive Viennese address since 1876 — family-owned, opera-facing, and the birthplace of the Sachertorte.
A restored 19th-century palace on Petersplatz where Mozart once lived — Rosewood's polished contemporary hand on the Old Town.

venues.a: Innere Stadt (1st), Am Hof / Goldenes Quartier
venues.d: A former bank turned calm, contemporary grand hotel in the luxury-shopping quarter — the spa pool sits in the old vault.

venues.n: Hotel Imperial, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A private palace of 1863 on the Ring — the grande dame that has housed nearly every head of state to visit Vienna.
Four linked 19th-century palaces on the Ring — Ritz-Carlton service behind a historic façade, with the city's best hotel rooftop bar.
A Theophil Hansen palace on the Ring, reborn under Anantara — grand bones, a serious spa, a Michelin kitchen within.

venues.n: Hotel Bristol, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A 1892 landmark facing the opera house — fin-de-siècle antiques, Austrian art, and a quietly grand sense of occasion.
Two neo-Baroque palaces across from the Stadtpark — suite-led, art-filled, with an original Klimt on the wall.
A small, discreet Relais & Châteaux townhouse a step from the opera — private, refined, all quiet luxury.
A design-led house beside the MuseumsQuartier — art on the walls, a fine spa, a younger sense of glamour.
One of the four historic grand hotels of the Ring — classical grandeur and a celebrated rooftop dining room.
The group's first Austrian house — a former court building reborn with Mandarin Oriental precision and a landmark spa.
A suites-only palace with one of the world's great wine cellars — and a two-star kitchen behind its columns.
A Renzo Piano-designed tower by the Belvedere gardens — contemporary, light, with a rooftop pool over the city.
A design hotel on the Ring between the opera and the Hofburg — contemporary art and an easy, central polish.
A theatrical, 1900s-Paris-inspired house with the city's most fashionable rooftop restaurant.
A Terence Conran-designed boutique beside the Albertina — warm, residential, beautifully made.
A characterful literary-themed townhouse just off the Ring — individual, well-priced, quietly charming.
A hidden design guesthouse on the first floor of a historic building — intimate, personal, central.
An art-filled townhouse hotel in the bohemian Spittelberg lanes — every room individually designed.
Heinz and Birgit Reitbauer's temple of modern Austrian cooking — one of only two three-star tables in the country.
Juan Amador's avant-garde cooking in the vaulted cellars of a Grinzing winery — Austria's other three-star.
Precise, contemporary cooking behind the columns of Palais Coburg — beside one of the world's great wine cellars.
Greek-Austrian roots and purist modern technique in a dark, elegant room with the kitchen in full view.
Lukas and Markus Mraz's witty, wildly individual cooking — Austria's most talked-about kitchen, and Falstaff's Chef of the Year.
Stefan Doubek won two stars before turning 32 — meticulous cooking over four live fires, with quiet Japanese influences.
Vegetarian fine dining that earned a star on its own terms — refined, seasonal, entirely meat-free.
A rare starred vegan kitchen — inventive, produce-led cooking that never feels like it's going without.
French technique and quiet ambition — one of the city's brightest recent stars, and a Falstaff favourite.
Creative, internationally-inflected tasting menus from a kitchen on a fast rise up the guides.
A former corner tavern turned surprise-menu star — casual on the surface, seriously good beneath.
Paul Gamauf's refined, produce-driven cooking inside the Palais Hansen on the Ring.
Modern cooking with Italian and Asian threads — a quietly assured one-star in the Old Town.
Modern cooking and a deep wine list in a smart room away from the tourist centre.
An avant-garde, ingredient-led kitchen with a cult following — precise, minimal, quietly radical.
South American technique meets Central European produce — a fresh, surprising one-star.
Classical fine dining on the Grand Hotel's roof — a long-held favourite for a dressed-up Viennese evening.
The city's most enduringly fashionable Italian — a see-and-be-seen room off the Graben.
A 1618 institution of Jugendstil tiles and open sandwiches — Viennese classics where the city has always gathered.
A buzzy, ink-ceilinged neighbourhood restaurant doing modern Viennese cooking with real flair.
Lively, informal Japanese cooking with modern turns — one of the most-loved everyday tables in the city.
Steirereck's relaxed little sister — a legendary goulash and a cheese counter to lose an afternoon to.
A tiny, warm tavern doing Austrian home cooking properly — the kind of room Vienna does best.
The temple of Tafelspitz — boiled beef in copper pots, carved and served with real ceremony.
Home of the schnitzel that overhangs the plate — a Viennese rite of passage since 1905.
Vienna's oldest inn, from 1447 — vaulted rooms where Beethoven, Schubert and Mark Twain all signed the wall.
TIAN's easy-going bistro — seasonal, regional vegetarian and vegan cooking at an everyday price.
The grand literary coffee house of Loos, Trotsky and Freud — vaulted, marble, and gloriously Viennese.
Vienna's most sophisticated coffee house since 1873 — the Ring café of politicians, writers and families.
The former imperial court confectioner, founded 1786 — part patisserie, part museum, entirely Viennese.
An 1880 coffee house barely changed in a century — billiard tables, newspapers, and the real, unhurried thing.

The Habsburgs' 1,441-room summer residence, all Rococo gilding and Maria Theresa yellow, with formal parterres climbing to the hilltop Gloriette. A private after-hours or Grand Tour guided visit spares multi-generational groups the queues, and the park's gravel walks are easy for elders and children alike.

The world's oldest zoo still in operation, founded in 1752, with giant pandas and giraffes housed inside original Baroque pavilions. A reliable multi-generational win — grandparents and small children both delighted — set within the palace grounds.

Six centuries of Habsburg power in one sprawling complex of 18 wings and 19 courtyards, still the working seat of the Austrian president. The Imperial Apartments and Sisi Museum tell the real story of Empress Elisabeth beyond the films.

Empress Elisabeth's private world inside the Hofburg — her gymnastics equipment, death mask and the reconstructed court silver — laid out through Franz Joseph's living and audience rooms. A tightly curated hour that fascinates teenagers as much as elders.

The white Lipizzaner stallions performing haute école dressage in Fischer von Erlach's chandelier-lit Winter Riding School, a tradition unbroken since the 18th century. Book the gala performance, or the quieter morning training session with a private box for the family.

Prince Eugene's Baroque summer palace holds the world's largest Klimt collection — including 'The Kiss' in its own gilded room — above formal gardens sweeping down to the Lower Belvedere. The palace terrace offers one of the loveliest framed views of the city skyline.

The quieter half of the Belvedere estate — Prince Eugene's private state rooms, the Marble Hall and the Hall of Grotesques — used for changing exhibitions. Combine with a stroll through the tiered French garden between the two palaces.

The Habsburgs' imperial art collection — the world's greatest holding of Bruegel, plus Vermeer, Velázquez, Raphael and Titian — under a domed staircase Klimt himself decorated. The palatial café beneath the cupola is a destination in itself.

A former Habsburg residence above the opera holding one of the world's foremost graphic collections — Dürer's 'Young Hare', Monet, Picasso — shown alongside the restored imperial state rooms. Central, compact and elegant, ideal for a focused morning.

The world's largest Egon Schiele collection alongside Klimt's 'Death and Life' and a definitive survey of Viennese Modernism, in a luminous white cube in the MuseumsQuartier. The clearest single window into Vienna 1900.

Austria's largest museum of modern and contemporary art — Warhol, Picasso, Viennese Actionism — inside a windowless basalt monolith in the MuseumsQuartier. For collectors and design-minded travellers rather than first-timers.

Vienna's temple of design and decorative arts, from Wiener Werkstätte silver and Thonet bentwood to Klimt's full-scale Stoclet Frieze cartoons. Essential for anyone furnishing a home or drawn to craft; its garden bar is a stylish evening spot.

One of the world's largest cultural complexes — Leopold, mumok, the Kunsthalle and Baroque courtyards filled with the signature painted 'Enzi' loungers. A relaxed base to graze between museums, with cafés for those who prefer to sit while others tour.

Vienna's soaring Gothic heart, its 136-metre south tower the tallest church in Austria and its zigzag tiled roof a city emblem. Climb the 343 steps of the tower, or take the lift to the north tower with elders, and tour the catacombs below.

Fischer von Erlach's Baroque masterpiece, its green copper dome flanked by two Trajan-style columns, built as a vow after the 1713 plague. A panorama lift rises into the cupola for a close look at the frescoes — a rare vantage that thrills all ages.
A jewel-box Baroque oval tucked just off the Graben, with a gilded pulpit, trompe-l'oeil dome and free lunchtime organ recitals. A quiet, discreet pause in the middle of the shopping streets.

One of the world's leading opera houses, staging a different work almost every night with an orchestra drawn from the Vienna Philharmonic. Reserve a private box; the guided backstage tour and elegant intermission suppers suit families building an evening together.

The 'Golden Hall', home of the Vienna Philharmonic since 1870 and stage for the televised New Year's Concert, prized for acoustics considered among the finest on earth. A gilt-and-caryatid room where hearing a concert is the whole point of the trip for many.

The city's other great hall, a 1913 building with four auditoriums whose programme ranges beyond classical into jazz and world music. The choice for a more adventurous evening, from September through June.

An interactive sound museum in the former home of the Vienna Philharmonic, where you can 'conduct' a virtual orchestra and explore the physics of music. The rare cultural stop that genuinely absorbs children and grandparents at once.

venues.n: Vienna Boys' Choir at the Hofburgkapelle
venues.d: The choir founded in 1498 sings Sunday Mass in the Hofburg's Imperial Chapel, an intimate and moving ritual, and performs full concerts at its own MuTh hall. Reserved seats spare families the scramble for the small chapel.

The 5.3-km grand boulevard Franz Joseph laid over the old city walls, lined with the Opera, Parliament, City Hall, university and twin museums — the finest ensemble of 19th-century monumental architecture in Europe. Best seen from a private car or the vintage tram that circles it.

Theophil Hansen's Greek-temple statement of democracy, fronted by the Pallas Athene fountain and newly restored throughout. Guided tours reveal the columned halls; the rooftop terrace and its restaurant offer a fresh angle on the Ring.

A soaring neo-Gothic pile whose square hosts the year's great open-air events — the Christmas market, summer film festival and an ice-skating 'Dream on Ice' in winter. A lively family gathering point at every season.

Vienna's first public park along the river Wien, home to the gilded Johann Strauss II monument — the city's most photographed statue. A gentle, central green break with a pond and café, easy for every generation.

The former imperial private garden behind the Hofburg, with a Mozart monument in flowers and an Art Nouveau glass Palmenhaus sheltering a butterfly house and an elegant café-brasserie. A discreet, sheltered oasis a step from the Ring.
A formal French garden on the Ring with thousands of rose bushes framing the neoclassical Theseus Temple, best in June bloom. A romantic, quiet counterpoint to the grand buildings around it.

The great public park with its historic Giant Ferris Wheel of 1897, immortalised in 'The Third Man', turning slowly over the city. Hire a private gondola with dinner service, then let children loose in the funfair and adults walk the leafy central avenue.

Friedensreich Hundertwasser's riotously colourful 1985 municipal apartment block, with undulating floors, onion domes and trees growing from the windows. A quick, joyful photo stop that breaks up the imperial grandeur — best paired with the museum nearby.

The artist's own museum in a rebuilt Thonet furniture factory, its wavy floors and green façade a full immersion in his ecological, anti-straight-line philosophy. The permanent Hundertwasser collection plus rotating photography shows, with a garden café.

Vienna's great 1.5-km market of 120-plus stalls — spices, cheeses, olives, and Middle Eastern and Asian produce that make vegetarian and Indian-friendly dining genuinely easy. Graze the mezze and falafel counters; the Saturday flea market is a cult ritual.

The vaulted, cathedral-like coffeehouse where Trotsky and Freud once sat, now serving Melange and towering pastries under marble columns. Grand and famous — arrive early or reserve to avoid the queue with a group.

Freud's regular café on the Ring by the Burgtheater, a wood-panelled institution since 1873 with a broad terrace and a proper kitchen for lunch, not just cake. The most comfortable of the grand cafés for a leisurely multi-generational sit.

The plush café of the Hotel Sacher, home of the original 1832 Sachertorte, served behind the Opera in red-velvet rooms. The definitive Vienna cake ritual; the box of torte travels home well as a gift.

The former imperial court confectioner on the Kohlmarkt, where white-gloved staff serve pastries beneath mirrored salons and you can watch the bakers at work. Old-world theatre and superb sweets, moments from the Hofburg.

A near-untouched 1880 coffeehouse with billiard tables, newspaper racks and worn Thonet chairs — the archetype away from the tourist crush. The place to linger over an Einspänner and read, exactly as the Viennese do.

The elegant pedestrian spine of the old city, from the Baroque Plague Column down to the luxury houses of the Kohlmarkt — Cartier, Louis Vuitton and the like — ending at the Hofburg gate. Vienna's discreet address for shopping and window-strolling.

A pocket of cobbled Biedermeier lanes behind the MuseumsQuartier, full of small galleries, artisan shops, wine bars and a beloved Advent market. The 7th district at its most walkable and characterful — good for an unhurried afternoon.

A wine-village on the city's northern edge where growers pour their own Grüner Veltliner in leafy courtyards beside Biedermeier villas. A relaxed, convivial evening of new wine and buffet food; a private car up and back suits a larger party.

The Vienna Woods summit above the vineyards, with a sweeping terrace over the whole city and the Danube, plus a café for a gentle finish. The classic drive-up panorama — no exertion required, dazzling after dark.

Terraced vineyards on the city's edge where open-air wine taverns like Wieninger and Sirbu look straight down over Vienna at sunset. A quietly spectacular alternative to Grinzing for a glass with a view.

One of Europe's largest cemeteries, with honorary graves of Beethoven, Brahms, Schubert and the Strauss family clustered near a monumental Art Nouveau church. A surprisingly serene, parkland pilgrimage for music lovers.

The gold-domed 1898 manifesto of the Vienna Secession — 'To every age its art' over the door — sheltering Klimt's monumental Beethoven Frieze in the basement. A compact, essential stop for the Vienna 1900 story.

A UNESCO-listed stretch of the Danube between Melk and Krems, terraced with apricot orchards and world-class Grüner Veltliner and Riesling vineyards, threaded with river villages. A private car or chartered boat makes for a superb, unhurried day out of the city.

A vast ochre Benedictine abbey on a bluff over the Danube, its Baroque library and gilded church among Europe's great interiors. The natural anchor for a Wachau day, ideally reached before the tour coaches.

The blue-and-white Baroque abbey tower and the castle ruin where Richard the Lionheart was held make this the prettiest Wachau village. Walk its single lane, taste at a riverside cellar, then continue down the Danube.

The Slovak capital, its compact old town crowned by a hilltop castle, reached in 75 minutes by the fast Twin City Liner catamaran along the Danube. An easy second-country outing — carry passports, as it crosses a border.

A grand Augustinian monastery just outside the city, with the priceless enamelled Verdun Altar of 1181, imperial state rooms and one of Austria's oldest wineries in its cellars. A short, rich half-day with a wine tasting to close.

Prince Eugene's restored country palace on the Marchfeld plain, with terraced Baroque gardens, a working estate farm and animals that charm younger visitors. A calmer, greener imperial day trip than the city palaces.
Adolf Loos's 1908 jewel-box in onyx and marble — the first cocktail bar in Vienna, and a landmark of modern design.
A ring-the-bell speakeasy that tops the national bar rankings — inventive drinks and a warm, in-the-know room.
A polished modern cocktail bar with a Styrian accent — one of the very best drinks addresses in the city.
A backlit Old Town nook that has led Vienna's cocktail revival for a decade — clear, light spirits done beautifully.
A legendary, encyclopaedic hotel bar — hundreds of spirits and a bartender who has seen it all.
An apothecary-themed cocktail bar mixing with precision and theatre — a favourite of the city's drinks crowd.
The city's best hotel rooftop — cocktails over the Ringstrasse rooftops, with St Stephen's spire in the distance.

venues.a: Innere Stadt (1st), SO/ Vienna, Danube Canal
venues.d: A glass-walled 18th-floor bar under a vast coloured-glass ceiling — the widest view over the city.
